questions.q: Define verbal irony and give one example from everyday conversation (not from the textbook).
questions.a: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what they mean, often for humorous or emphatic effect. Example: Saying "Great job!" when someone drops a tray of food. A wrong answer (e.g., defining it as lying) reveals confusion between irony and deception—irony requires an audience that recognizes the contrast.

questions.q: Explain the difference between situational irony and dramatic irony in your own words.
questions.a: Situational irony: outcome contradicts expectations (e.g., a fire station burns down). Dramatic irony: audience knows something characters don't (e.g., we know the killer is behind the door). A wrong answer that swaps them shows the student hasn't internalized the role of audience knowledge vs. expectation reversal.

questions.q: In "Patterns of Creativity", the author describes a scientist as "playing with toys" while a poet is "building cathedrals". Identify the type of irony here and explain its effect.
questions.a: This is verbal irony—the author uses "playing with toys" to diminish science and "building cathedrals" to elevate poetry, but the essay's broader argument may undermine this hierarchy. The irony invites readers to question the labels. A wrong answer that calls it situational irony misses that the irony is in the language choice, not an event outcome.

questions.q: The essay repeatedly mentions "the prism" as an image. Analyze how the prism functions as a symbol for the relationship between science and poetry.
questions.a: A prism splits white light into colors (science) but also creates beauty (poetry); it symbolizes unity in diversity—the same source yielding different patterns. A wrong answer that only says "it represents light" fails to connect the symbol to the essay's central theme of complementary creativity.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the irony in the essay strengthens or weakens the author's argument about the patterns of creativity. Justify your view.
questions.a: The irony strengthens the argument by exposing false dichotomies: when the author ironically calls science "mere classification", the reader senses the oversimplification and is primed for the nuanced synthesis. A wrong answer that says "it weakens because it's confusing" misses irony's rhetorical purpose of engaging critical thinking.

questions.q: Create a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) describing a symbolic object from your own life (e.g., a family heirloom, a tree) and use verbal irony to comment on its significance.
questions.a: A good answer will name an object, explain its symbolic meaning (e.g., a neem tree = resilience), and include a verbally ironic statement (e.g., "This 'useless' tree that only gives shade and medicine"). A poor answer will lack either the symbolic explanation or the ironic contrast, showing incomplete grasp of combining devices.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between ______ and reality, often revealing a deeper truth.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're reading "Patterns of ______" and notice the author says one thing but means another, or an object like a "bridge" keeps appearing.
What is Irony? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between expectation and reality, often revealing a deeper truth.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Irony?
questions.a: Students often confuse symbolism with metaphor, thinking any comparison is a symbol.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify and explain at least two types of irony (verbal, situational, dramatic) and two symbols in the essay "Patterns of Creativity", and write a structured analytical paragraph using the PEEL method for each device.
